fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces modulation-period/interface-coherency control with temperature-induced short-range ordering and therefore does not reconstruct the central intervention or mediator.
Temperature directly changes thermally activated creep, so the proposed comparison cannot isolate SRO as the cause of any creep-rate difference.
The claim that lower temperature or higher strain rate will generate consequential SRO in these Al-Cr-Fe-Ni FCC/BCC multilayers is not established by the cited evidence.
No prediction is made for the distinctive semicoherent 16 nm multilayer, its minimum stress exponent, or its superior creep resistance relative to coherent and grain-boundary-dominated baselines.
explanation: The response addresses sustained deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayers and offers a testable alternative involving SRO-mediated dislocation pinning. However, it misses the target's governing variable: modulation period determines whether coherent interfaces, semicoherent interfaces with misfit dislocations, or grain boundaries dominate. It consequently omits the proposed pileup-induced interfacial amorphization and diffusion/interface-slip mechanism, as well as the observed nonmonotonic optimum at 16 nm and stress-exponent transition. Its baseline is poorly specified and lacks the 8, 32, and 80 nm controls. The cited studies support SRO strengthening in other alloy systems and mechanically induced ordering under specialized 77 K tensile conditions, but they do not validate SRO evolution during room-temperature indentation creep in the target coating. The proposed temperature comparison is also intrinsically confounded because temperature affects creep kinetics independently of SRO. A stronger test would independently prepare measurably different SRO states while holding phase structure, interfaces, grain size, temperature, and loading history constant, then determine whether creep rates and stress exponents track SRO.
